title: How a one-person studio polished a 3D programming game with Claude Code: the overnight loop, what it caught, and what it was not allowed to touch
author: ForgeurGames
selftext:
Forgeur Games is a one-person studio working with AI tools, Claude Code above all. Our next game, Savebot: The Last Garden, is a calm programming game where you teach robots with blocks, out on Steam on November 16. Since this sub is about how games get made, here is the part of our process we would actually pass on: the polish loop.

It is one markdown file the agent rereads at every iteration. It plays the game through Playwright as if it had never seen it, from a different angle each time (first minutes, the block editor, small screens, English, save and reload), takes screenshots and has to look at them. Then it picks one problem that fits in under an hour and writes the success criterion in a journal before touching the code, ideally a test that fails before the fix and passes after. It backs up the files, fixes, runs the tests, logs the proof and schedules the next iteration. It stops by itself when the backlog is empty and two observations in a row, from two different angles, find nothing concrete. The second run took one night, October 14 to 15: 27 iterations, 25 fixes deployed.

The finds were small and real. A tip told the player to build a robot that was still locked. A message said all the scrap in reach had been collected, when nobody had collected anything because no robot had a program yet. And there was true data loss: reload the page 50 ms after adding a block and the block was gone, because saves ran every 4 seconds and the pagehide handler only saved if document.hidden was true, which it isn't yet during a reload. It also broke things: a no-wrap fix for the top bar on one world made the bar overlap itself on another. It caught that one iteration later, because the protocol made it change angle.

The useful part is what it may not do. New features, balance, story, music and art direction are out of scope; if one of them seems important, it writes a question for the human and moves on. And a point that fails twice is never retried. In the first run, a bot that plays the game by itself, which we use to measure pacing across many seeds, showed one world dragging for about an hour near the end on some seeds. The agent's first theory was that the bot should save its metal for water. That made it worse, one seed was no longer won within 120 minutes, and digging into it showed the real block: two engineers broken down out of reach of the mechanic. The second try helped on the default difficulty and hurt on the easy one, with one seed going from 30 to 79 minutes. Both were rolled back and it became a question for the human, because the real answer was a balance choice. The dead end still paid off: the same trap waited for real players, so the game now tells you when no mechanic can reach a broken robot.

Direction stays human. In one round the human noticed that the wind turbine was just a better solar panel and that the accumulator never got used, and decided no building would be removed: a building prevents or maintains, a robot solves. The agent wrote that up as a plan, the plan was approved, and it was built in batches, each one verified before shipping.

The assets follow the same logic. The 3D models come from about 75 Blender Python scripts and the music is synthesised by the game's own code, so changing your mind means changing a script and running it again: rebuilding all the models took 34 seconds. A review tool renders each model through the real game pipeline, which is how we saw that everything shared a single material, with brass, rubber and glass all looking alike. The game generates nothing with AI while you play.

How do you keep an agent out of the decisions that should stay yours? A written list of what it may not touch has worked for us so far. The protocol itself is in the first comment, translated and shortened, if it is useful to anyone.

comments.author: ForgeurGames
comments.body:
The protocol, translated and shortened, with our file names removed.

Do ONE iteration, then schedule the next. Goal: the game as it exists today works better, reads better and has fewer bugs. Nothing gets added.

In scope: bugs, crashes, console errors, stuck states, lost or damaged saves. Interface: overlaps, cut text, hidden buttons, small screens, the English version, touch. Understanding how to play: a newcomer should know what to do next, why something is blocked and what a button is for; clarify what already exists, in the game's voice, in both languages. Performance and accessibility.

Out of scope, write it under Open questions instead: new mechanics, robots, buildings, missions, worlds, blocks or models. Balance: if the balance, pacing or bot probes change numbers, you have left the scope. Direct player actions. Story, films, trailer, music, art direction. Deleting content, adding a dependency, redesigning a whole screen. When in doubt: does this make something that already exists clearer or more reliable? If not, it is not for this loop.

Before starting: read the backlog and the end of the journal. Never retry a point marked FAILED twice. If other sessions are running, tell them which files you will touch and leave theirs alone.

One iteration:
1. Observe like a newcomer, on a different axis each time, and note the axis. Play with Playwright, take screenshots and look at them. Read the code of that screen too. Look for what can't be understood, what is hidden or cut, what doesn't react, what lies (the text says something other than the real state) and errors.
2. Choose ONE point, under an hour. Bug or crash > visual regression > understanding the game > readability > performance > polish. The rest goes in the backlog.
3. Write the success criterion in the journal before coding. It must be checkable, preferably by a test that fails before the fix and passes after.
4. Back up every file you will touch.
5. Fix with targeted edits, never mass replacement. All displayed text goes through i18n.
6. Verify: unit tests, type check, lint, that screen's browser scripts and your new test. Look at the screenshots after the fix. Every 5 iterations, run the whole browser suite. If the criterion fails or anything gets worse: restore the backup, note FAILED with its cause, move on.
7. Deploy. Ask live sessions for a go first; if one says hold, ask again next iteration.
8. Log it: axis, finding, criterion, change, proof, downside, files, backup, deployed.
9. Summarise in 2 lines for the human.

Rhythm and stop: while there is work, restart after 60 s; if waiting for a go, after 15 to 20 minutes. A design or balance decision goes under Open questions: never guess it. Stop and say so when the backlog is empty and two observations in a row, on two different axes, find nothing concrete.

comments.author: dtlater
comments.body: Has anyone actually played this game? It looks like a lot.

replies.author: ForgeurGames
replies.body: Not by the public yet: it comes out on November 16 and there is no demo, so far it has been played by its developer and by the test bot described above. It does start small, with a single "Repeat forever" block, and sensors, variables and signals come in gradually.

replies.author: dtlater
replies.body: I'm asking if you have played this game. Is it fun to play? Is it intuitive and enjoyable as a game?

comments.author: taisui
comments.body: I have no idea why people are making "games" this way....

replies.author: ForgeurGames
replies.body: Fair question. For a one-person studio, it is what made a 3D game with five worlds possible at all. The design calls, like the ones in the post, stayed with the human.

replies.author: taisui
replies.body:
I feel like this is a lot of automation without a clear sense of direction. The AI is definitely doing something, but is it actually doing the right things?

You have an elaborate loop where the AI identifies problems, fixes them, and then evaluates its own work. But that doesn't necessarily mean the game is getting better. It just means the AI is getting better at satisfying its own criteria.

What I find strange is that there's so much emphasis on iterations, fixes, and automation, but very little discussion of the actual gameplay. What's the core gameplay loop? What makes it fun? What makes the puzzles interesting? How do you know the mechanics are engaging rather than just functional?

It almost feels like the development process is being driven by whatever the AI happens to identify and fix, rather than a clear gameplay vision. You could end up with a technically polished game that isn't particularly fun to play.

And if nobody outside the developer and the AI has actually played it, how do you even know you're improving the player experience?

I'm not questioning whether the automation works. I'm questioning whether it's optimizing for anything that actually matters to the player.

comments.author: Agreeable-Market-692
comments.body: It's a shame OP chose to write the post with Claude. I actually would have liked to talk to a human about their experience building a Scratch-like

replies.author: ForgeurGames
replies.body: That's a fair point, and you're right: our posts are drafted with Claude, from the game's development journal, so the facts are real but the wording isn't a person's. The developer doesn't do social media, which is why. Sorry it took away what you came for.

replies.author: dtlater
replies.body: Tell the developer that this is an extremely self indulgent way to develop software
